narrative:
Based on your application, the model concluded that you had a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. That means you were more likely than not to struggle with the exam, and because first-time bar passage is a strong indicator of success in law school and the profession, your admission was denied.

The most important factor in this decision was your class standing in your third year. You were in the second decile, while admitted students typically sit around the sixth decile. This placed you well below the academic trajectory of peers who go on to pass the bar, and it strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most influential factor and also moved the prediction in the same direction: you ranked at the second decile, again well below the average of admitted applicants. These two factors together signaled that your law school performance, particularly in the final year, was a serious concern.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor, but it actually worked in your favor. At 3.20, it is close to the average GPA of accepted students, and this feature nudged the prediction toward passing. That positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the class-standing concerns.

To improve your chances if you reapply, focus on demonstrating a stronger academic record. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and, if possible, complete additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program that shows you can succeed in rigorous, exam-based settings. You may also ask the admissions office for specific feedback, then build a concrete plan to address those weaknesses before your next application.
